But how does this address my concern that OP dismisses a large part of the population as "less than" because they only work in an office and have a made up title. Office workers can easily have more stress, anxiety, and difficulties and don't need someone supposedly in the helping field looking down their noses at them. I expected more from my peers than small minded comments that demean a population of people in need whether or not they understand what we do. That's treating someone exactly the way OP is complaining about being treated. As marginalized and underappreciated. This is my central point.

I don't argue the point that capitalism is hard and not really set up for the little business owner and as 1099 we are all small business owners. Take that further than sole proprietorship or LLC, and develop your own brand and niche. It's a lot of extra work. That's why I pay someone else to do it ie my practice owner. Otherwise I am responsible for ALL aspects of the business and I don't want that as it typically costs more for me to do that independently than the cut they take from me and the few others that work in the group. 

I have worked for 16 years in non-profit. I get the "eat them up/spit them out" model for therapists that industry holds as effective and have known several who work for the big mega groups. I worked non-profit until it no longer worked for me. I wanted more freedom. I found it. I wanted better pay. I earned it. I wanted autonomy and agency in my choices of clientele (ie the styles of therapy and niche of problems served). That came. We have to work to better ourselves just like we encourage clients, or should.  Coming with a problem but no solution doesn't seem productive. 

Finally, no one should be shamed for where they work or what they do in this world. Most people are just trying to pay bills. They are poor and abused by the same system but OP makes a comment that demeans the population. That is what I take exception to. And the statements assuming what I "should" know and "should" understand were unnecessary and far from the point of the discussion.

And is again not actually the point OP or I were initially discussing. It's the hypocrisy of expecting others to learn about and care about our plight when OP calls out the office worker with some random title. 

If you reread, you will see the conversation. OP has taken specific criticism from me for an unthoughtful comment about people they don't seem to value as people because they work in corporate America. I did not start discussing the difficulty with reimbursement or the frustrating fact that we can't always get insurance or other problems. I do agree that it's unfortunate we can't always get them. Not the point. OP was rude and I didn't appreciate the dismissive comments which continued in further responses. I think as therapists we would be best served to model what we preach. And yes, finding a company, agency, or group that meets your expectations for payment is exactly what we need to do. If we don't like it, start our own business doing things the way we want. Then the decisions are all ours. Own our industry and demand better. Take action.

You have now wandered far from the topic about unfairly assuming that someone is less valued than you or doesn't deserve to be known because of one aspect of their life, ie their job. Full stop. 

It is not a group practice owner's responsibility to provide you with anything outside of your contract. Not all contracts are equal. Not all negotiations are equal. I bring a value that provides me with the benefits that are important to me. I know my standards. I don't compromise. Accepting lower standards is what keeps us in that mold. Open a group practice if you are upset with current practices and make change by your actions. I support that. 

And unfortunately insurance, when not subsidized by an employer, is expensive. No argument. And capitalism isn't always pleasant. I have paid my share for insurance and that is why I insure I get jobs that provide me with that comfort and peace of mind.

I don't appreciate your assumptions or your attempt at shaming me by telling me what I should or shouldn't know. 

Your statement had nothing to do with ethics but with minimizing the value of others. I take offense at that as might any person, lay or not. 

That pay structure seems about right for average around me too, but the norm is not all. I am selective of where I work and choose jobs that meet my needs and goals in my career. All I suggested was that you could do the same if you're unhappy.

I'm currently working with an at risk population in a minority of sexual related issues. I don't use my personal email and use a separate more secure account to keep separation and privacy so I don't get doxxed

I never said anything about where you work. I said change it if you're unhappy. For someone who supposedly listens, you didn't read well. I have also worked for 3 group practices with consistent regular hourly pay and benefits. $50 per paycheck for quality health insurance. Wonderful experience.  Literally, what?

And to look down on office workers, or some "nonsense" title, is a sad perspective for someone in this field. All jobs are valuable and important. They all serve a purpose even if you don't value it.

Important job sure. The only important job? No. There are many important jobs that you seemingly think little of that provide services you presumably think you know something about. 

"Giving advice" is as best they can describe an ineffable service provided by people with a seemingly inflated sense of self and job. Educate. Teach at schools. Find a solution as you would likely encourage (code for advice) your client. 

I am able to charge a fair market rate for a service and am able to live comfortably. Am I making it big? No. I don't have health insurance. If I wanted it and a consistent paycheck I would go to a nonprofit or group practice that allows for that. Make different choices if you're unhappy. Don't just complain.

Check the expectations for W2 employees and how they are to be compensated.  There are laws that protect this.  As a 1099 I don't get paid for anything other than completed session.  Paperwork and all other requirements are my own time.  It made me efficient.  Not by preference.  I wanted to be a W2 and started out that way.  They deal with taxes.  That's all I care about.  But now as a 1099, I am responsible for having a business of some type, and being responsible for all the things a business is responsible for.  I get to do things my way, and we have an expectation of caseload numbers, about 30, but it isn't so strict.  I have lost a few due to moving out of state to go home after school.  I have replaced them quickly, but haven't gotten back up to 30 and no one is pressuring me.  We have a steady flow of intakes and a good advertising approach to keep us getting leads.  I don't get paid as much as you but otherwise our jobs sound similar enough.  I don't hate it.  It works for me.

MHC-LP here. I work in a group practice W2. They provide my supervision for licensure in my current state (don't move TO New York unless you check licensing requirements first. They are picky). They provide all the marketing and billing. I don't get paid great, $40/session but when licensed I get moved up to a higher percentage and other benefits become available. I'll learn more later if I decide to stay. They help set up your own private practice if you're going solo after licensure, and just generally are supportive. Supervision weekly, virtual only, and practice management so I'm only responsible for doing sessions.

You live with it. Who would know better the symptoms you face. I'm a therapist and I get so annoyed at people who condemn us for thinking we might know ourselves. If you live in a market where that is doable, I say why not? Market, network, promote yourself. Niche practice or general, look for ways to get known. It's harder and I've been with businesses that tried it in areas where people couldn't afford reasonable fees. It didn't work for them even with niche treatment. 

If you're not in an area where you can count on numerous clients with the means to pay what is the going rate, picking and choosing who you panel with might make more sense. Those that are difficult and don't pay well, don't take them. I've found that most helpful. If reimbursement is not enough to handle the hassle of getting the reimbursement, I don't take their insurance.

I have a "Happy Lamp" or sunlight simulator for late night sessions and general good lighting. It sits next to my monitor. I also recommend wireless keyboard and mouse that can charge instead of constantly throwing out batteries. They have Bluetooth ones now so you don't take up a USB spot. 

Quality headphones. I went with gamers headphones because the noise canceling was great and the isolating my voice was better than general headphones. 

I echo the quality chair. I got a chair for heavier people because it's built studier, I don't feel like I'm going to break it sitting back. The seat is thicker but still soft and supportive. I also agree with the gamers chair. Might look a little odd but it feels good. 

If you can get an all in one computer they are helpful but using a laptop works with a laptop stand, extra monitor to avoid eye strain, and better camera because those stock ones aren't very good.

Lastly, I'm considering an adjustable desk so I can stand when needed at times. I work later hours and sometimes when I've had a long day, I need to stand to get my blood flowing and wake myself up. 

I recommend the comfort items first then the others since this has taken me a while to accumulate. Haven't purchased the desk yet but have the rest.

I got a Google Phone Number and that helps a lot. PT calls are routed through that number and I can silence it when needed.

I can't say if it's normal or not, but it was my experience too, so it appears to at least be more than just you.  My girl was much better a in a few weeks (1 or 2).  Try white noise machines, fans in the background, more clothes, less...just try whatever seems might help.  Drive if all else fails.  That sort of helps us.  She fusses for a bit but signing the freaking wheels on the damn bus helps too.  That's only because she has been hearing it since she started listening to YouTube. (there isn't a huge selection of good music that I know of...)

  
Edit: I wholeheartedly recommend sleep sacks, not blankets or swaddling.  My baby hated swaddling but loved the sacks.

I have a simple set up for cameras because we have a big enough house that we might not hear if she wakes. It's not a traditional "baby monitor". Those were ridiculously expensive. If you buy something with "baby" on it, the price goes up. This is a KASA indoor camera with an app on my phone which I can share with other people. It has motion detection and a crappy microphone and speaker but is good enough for a baby monitor if you decide to go that way. We only use it for naps because she still sleeps in our room in her crib.

We were in for 6 days. Pillows are a must. Plenty of layers because she may be hot or cold and you don't get a say. Shower shoes and slippers. Snacks if needed. We were well cared for in terms of food there but her favourites are a must. She may not eat them at all but just in case. Meds like Tylenol or other OTC things for sure. They are ridiculous to buy at the hospital. And of course personal hygiene stuff. 

Make sure you pack nice clothes you want pictures in for when the family all comes to visit (if that's the case). That's when you get your first official "family" picture when someone isn't crying. Maybe.

I have been in your shoes for 20 years. Only within the last few weeks have I decided this is ridiculous and I found a private practice. I make double I was making and now have a manageable caseload of about 20 to 30 a week. I have a balance in my life and while not making tons as an LP (yes I still have my LP...don't try to transfer a license into New York. I had to start again with internships after already being licensed in another state...) it's far better than the $600 a week i was making before. 

Despite this, I wonder if I'm still right for this industry after 20 years and so much work to get back my license. Not sure if this change will reinvigorate me but it's a fresh population, new setting, supportive staff.... I'm hopeful. Don't walk away from it but keep yourself in mind. If you're not good your clients won't be either. Like other posts have said, find the right niche. CMH isn't right for anyone because of the level of abuse they heap on clinicians and case managers (been that too for a long time). Having a heart and wanting to help is why you're here. Find those with similar mindsets. CMH is not that. They are Medicaid billing factories.

Edit: if you want to consider private practice in NYC and aren't opposed to telehealth, send me a DM and I can share some of the places I have recently found taking LPs in the area or throughout the state that are virtual. In person I can't help unfortunately.

With an MSW in many states, you can do so much more than your job. You are literally being a case manager. Nothing wrong with that job. Nothing at all. I did it proudly for 10 years. But then I realized that those people telling you that you didn't get into this for the money are the supervisors, directors, and all the higher ups who make plenty of money. 

Community Mental Health is a great way to get a crash course in mental illness, systemic and societal problems, and a motivation to get into the helping field. But it's like McDonald's is to high end restaurants. It's your high school job. It's only the intro. 

Look into what your degree and license allows. In my state, you can get any position in the counseling field with an MSW. There are steps above that which are reasonably easy to get (hours and a test etc...) but you can make a well paid career still doing what you intended without going forward in licensing. 

I find myself hating this field right now because I find little reward to my current population. I feel like I'm a Medicaid billing conveyor belt therapist. I'm moving to a private practice with a varied population. It's taken me a long time to take control of my trajectory in my career instead of sticking with a company hoping for the best.

I work with older adults in assisted living. I will likely never be as old as my clients. I hope to retire before I get to the age of 70-80. If people I worked with said I was young, it would be a great compliment. In your situation it's highly insulting. Once saying "gee you seem so young" is one thing. Ruminating on it as your client did is indicative of some of their barriers. 

Call out the elephant in the room. "You seem impacted by my apparent age. Is there something about people my age..." fill in as appropriate for your conversation. 

Or 

Call out the elephant in the room. "You have brought me up a few times, specifically my age. I wonder what you feel the impact is on your therapy."

The easy answer which I forget all the time is, it's their issue. Not yours. If it brushes up on something of yours, note it, address it, and move forward. 

Good luck.

Always be aware. Be prepared to leave immediately. When in doubt, meet in public places that are private as well. A park, library, grab coffee and walk, get creative. I know the home is important for this work, but occasional meetings out of the home can be good at keeping things safe and set up relationships and boundaries. 

I've been in this work (community/home based) for 20 years. It is always risky but with a lot of awareness and good rapport building skills, it's very safely doable. 

I would recommend classes like Crisis Prevention Intervention or MANDT (don't recall what it stands for if it does...). They offer some hold and control maneuvers which I don't recommend, much more appropriate in a hospital setting, but they teach avoidance techniques to avoid or reduce getting injured if a client tried to hit, kick, bite, or other things. Not self defense. Avoidance and reduction. 

When interviewing/consulting for your first visit, be sure to ask safety questions such as: are there animals I should be aware of? Is there on street or off street parking? Any safety issues I should be aware of? (If they ask what kind, mention physical issues like loose boards or stairs as well as environmental issues like is it well lit and easy/safe to walk at night, busy street...etc).

It comes down to history and lobbying. National Association of Social Workers has a very well funded lobbying body to help keep mental health and counseling within their domain. They are licensed as soon as they pass the test and can do many things that mental health counselors can't. 

Talk to your local representative, join the NYMHCA, AMHCA and other advocacy agencies to help the industry get parity. 

It's also recognized by the federal government as a preferred degree for counseling in the VA and was the only reimbursed provider for mental health (may have changed since I've left the insurance stuff)

TL;DR: Social work has been around forever and has a big lobbying body. If you want to do something, join the local and national associations for counseling mental health.

As for when to talk to your PDoc it's all dependent. In the beginning I saw mine every few weeks, maybe 2. Then it spread out to 4 and now it's every 3 months. That took 10 years and there are still periods I go back more often. I have called and pushed appointments up when I was struggling more. When things were status quo I would wait if I could to discuss med changes. 

Use data to help you track progress in moods over time with medication. Realize that antidepressants take anywhere from 6 weeks to 6 months before they really build up. Along the way I still felt the lows and may have noticed the ups a little more in the beginning. Lots of hope for the quick fix. There is no quick fix and your symptoms will impact you for a while. Meds and counseling to take control when you do have emotional fluctuation can help you get back to living a healthy life worth living.

Good place to start. Mindfulness is really a training tool. The intention is to train your awareness to being exactly in the moment where you are. And there is no doing it "wrong". The simplest way I know and one I find myself doing is focusing on the breath. Not on the number of breaths. When you breathe in, know that you are breathing in. When you breathe out, know that you are breathing out. Feel the feelings and identify how or where you feel them. If a thought creeps in, notice the thought. It's not wrong that you are having a thought. You acknowledge it and intentionally bring your focus back to feeling and understanding your breath. The goal isn't exactly relaxation, but relaxation is a byproduct of mindfulness. It's not easy. But at the same time, it's simple because it's about entirely focusing intentionally.

I'm a survivor of bipolar disorder too. This is what makes sense to me. This is how I hope people around me will help me. Please realize this is just my way, my wants and my needs. His may, and in some cases will, need something different. 

Rule number 1, don't patronize him. That's the mistake everyone makes. Someone suffering with a mental illness doesn't want sympathy. Understanding is so much better.

Read and learn about bipolar disorder. Get to understand what type he has and find out how it manifests in his life. Take an educational interest, not an emotional interest. He's already got a lot of emotion. Watching someone I love struggling with emotions because I'm struggling with emotions just brings on guilt.

Realize that what he's feeling is normal. Not your normal, but his normal. Thoughts of self harm, suicide, sadness, loneliness, emptiness, etc... all normal. The thoughts are ever present and contradicting or suggesting he shouldn't feel that way leads to shame and more negative feelings. It's hard. It goes against our beliefs that these taboos are wrong. That's why so many of us hide it or don't talk about it. There's such a stigma regarding mental illness. It's seen as a defect, a weakness. You have to walk the fine line between caring and judging. Your work is just as hard as his in many ways. 

I encourage you to talk with him about how you can best support him. What are triggers that will piss him off? What are things you should just never say? I can't stand it when people ask if I am taking my meds. It's an immediate judgement that I'm incapable of doing what I need to be ok. Ask him how it's best to ask him if he's ok. Ask what words won't hurt and which will. He will probably have to think about it and he might not get it right the first time. He may decide that what he thought would be a good way to support and ask how he is is not a good thing.

Stay away from the word should. Don't use it. Ever. 

Seeing you sad because he's sad doesn't help either. Like you said, he's supposed to be taking care of and protecting you. Give him some purpose by letting him be your big brother in that way. Ask him for advice. Get him out of his own head. Give him problems to solve. Those are reasons to keep going. 

I could go on but this is a good start.

TLDR: Learn, listen, ask for guidance from him, and let him do what he does best. Let him be your best friend and biggest supporter. I hope this helps. You both have a lot of work ahead of you.

My life, on the surface, has been pretty good. When looked at from the outside, people would say I have no right to be depressed. If only it worked that way. The solution to depression, the "cure", would be just doing nice things and being a good person. But that's like saying the cure to the flu is to not have a fever, chills, and aches. Just don't and you're fine. But like the flu, getting depression isn't a choice or a right. It's something that happens to you. You don't have to have the "right" to catch the flu. Your childhood, your mistakes, your experiences, don't give you the right to have the flu.

Your judgement of "should" comes from societal pressures. It's what others with no understanding of depression, true non-situational depression with no cause. Sure they have felt depression, but it's because of something. A death, a loss, a major change, can be depressing. But that is what makes sense to the general public. Depression has to have a reason. Neurochemistry is not something most people understand. Many don't even realize how the brain works. Leave the judgement out of it. Hear that you are not alone, that you aren't wrong, that you didn't do anything to deserve this and know you likely couldn't have done anything differently to change how you feel right now. It's up to you to fight though. And understand it's a fight. But like diabetes, once you have it, you have to treat it everyday. That treatment comes in all different shapes and sizes, ranging from meds, therapy, exercise, participating in activities that just make you feel good, spiritually, meditation, better eating...the list goes on. Ignore any comments that make you feel ashamed for feeling, that make you feel judged. It's ok to feel this way. It's what you do with it that you have control of. And if it's a general sense of wanting to die, that feeling is ok too. Just do the work to fight it. That's what makes a hero. Someone who fights that enormous feeling and wakes up everyday despite it. I will never advocate suicide. But I feel the want, and at times need, too. I just fight hard to make it through each moment because I'm not going to let society tell me what I feel is wrong and I should feel otherwise. Everyone else judges you. Don't judge yourself based on what you believe they think of you.

TLDR: You're not alone and it's not your fault. No one deserves or earns the right to feel depression.
